events.title: World: Speed, Scale and Disregard: How new technology and changing tactics are driving civilian harm
events.summary: Countries: World, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Iran (Islamic Republic of), Lebanon, occupied Palestinian territory, Sudan, Ukraine Source: Norwegian Refugee Council Please refer to the attached file. Authors: Jenny McAvoy I Chris Rogers I Emanuela Gillard War is changing. The risks to civilians are changing with it. From the destruction of critical civilian infrastructure to the growing use of drones and AI-assisted targeting systems, evolving patterns of warfare are exposing civilians to devastating and far-reaching harm. Drawing on research across six contexts where the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) supports people affected by displacement, this report examines how and why civilians are being harmed - and what can be done to protect them. Across the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Gaza, the Islamic Republic of Iran, Lebanon, Sudan and Ukraine, it identifies two particularly concerning trends: the widespread destruction of infrastructure, disrupting access to essential services, and the growing use of emerging military technologies, raising new challenges for civilian protection and compliance with international humanitarian law. Much of the resulting suffering is foreseeable and can be prevented or reduced. Reversing this trajectory requires action from parties to conflict and the states that support them. The report calls for greater use of political, military and economic leverage to strengthen compliance with international humanitarian law and efforts to mitigate civilian harm; improved military practices and oversight; earlier investment in restoring damaged civilian infrastructure; and better documentation and analysis of civilian harm to inform efforts to protect civilians.

Author: Ahmad Zia Wahdat, PhD Between 2021 and October 2026, about 7.2 million Afghans returned from Iran, Pakistan and elsewhere, and one in seven people now living in Afghanistan is a returnee. This independent report by Data for Afghanistan places every returnee in one of Afghanistan's 401 districts. It then measures that number against the people, inhabited land, public health workers, wages, rent and prices already there. It draws only on open and publicly accessible data from IOM, UNHCR, the Ministry of Public Health, WFP and the National Statistics and Information Authority. It introduces a district typology that separates two kinds of pressure: the returnee share of residents and spatial crowding (returnees per km² of inhabited land). The report also includes a stress test for a further one million returnees, recommendations for organizations, and profiles of all 34 provinces with district-level tables. Return is highly concentrated. Ten districts hold 21% of all returnees, and in Kunduz, Daykundi and Herat close to one resident in four is a returnee. In "saturated" districts, both the returnee share and crowding are above the national average, and 45% of returnees live in these districts. Entre enero y agosto de 2026, Colombia continuó enfrentando una crisis humanitaria marcada por la acumulación de impactos del conflicto armado y de eventos de origen natural recurrentes. La situación se agravó tras el terremoto de agosto , que incrementó las necesidades humanitarias en territorios que ya enfrentaban los efectos de la violencia, la pobreza y una limitada presencia institucional. Esta combinación de emergencias puso aún más presión sobre las capacidades de respuesta de las autoridades locales y nacionales. La intensificación de las hostilidades y el control territorial de grupos armados siguen deteriorando las condiciones de vida de comunidades rurales y étnicas. Los confinamientos, restricciones a la movilidad y limitaciones de acceso a bienes esenciales persisten como una de las afectaciones más críticas, incrementando riesgos de protección, inseguridad alimentaria y vulneración de derechos. El terremoto de magnitud 7,4 ocurrido en agosto evidenció la fragilidad de territorios ya vulnerables y donde las capacidades de respuesta locales ya enfrentaban desafíos y limitaciones. Más allá de la emergencia inmediata, el sismo incrementó las necesidades , mientras confirmó la urgencia de fortalecer la preparación, resiliencia comunitaria y capacidad de respuesta frente a crisis complejas y concurrentes. events.title: UNHCR Jordan: Zaatari Informal Market Dynamics (2024 – 2026)
events.summary: Countries: Jordan, Syrian Arab Republic Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees Please refer to the attached file. The Zaatari Informal Market has played an important role in supporting refugee livelihoods, providing essential goods and services, and facilitating economic activity within the camp since its establishment. Emerging organically in response to refugees’ livelihood needs, the market developed into a central economic space along the main commercial streets of the camp, hosting a wide range of businesses operated by refugees. Yet, with close to one third of Syrian refugees having left Jordan to return to Syria since the change of government in Syria in December 2024, the population of Zaatari camp has shrunk from nearly 76,000 to around 43,0671 , affecting the overall camp economic activity. This analysis examines the evolution and transformation of the Zaatari Informal Market between December 2024 and June 2026, based on business tracking 2024 baseline data covering 1,507 surveyed shops, across three assessment rounds (December 2024 baseline, December 2025, and June 2026). events.title: Five key lessons from multi-hazard preparedness in Nigeria
events.summary: Country: Nigeria Source: ODI - Humanitarian Practice Network Olayinka Afolabi Nigeria does not lack information about humanitarian risk. Flood forecasts, conflict analysis, disease surveillance and community reports regularly identify where threats are increasing. The more salient question is whether that information changes what institutions do before people are affected. I confronted this question while serving as UNICEF’s technical focal point in support of government-led emergency preparedness processes. These included the 2021 Nigeria Countrywide Risk Analysis , its 2024 update , the National Contingency Plan and preparedness exercises in the Northwest. The analyses covered all 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory and examined risks at local-government level. The national plan subsequently provided an overarching framework across Nigeria’s six geopolitical zones, with State Emergency Management Agencies expected to adopt and adapt it. This was important progress. Yet our experience also showed that producing an analysis or plan is only the beginning. During preparedness work, the same questions kept returning. Who has authority to act on a warning? Which locations should be prioritised? How will state plans reach local government areas and communities? Are supplies available, and who can release them? What happens to agreed actions after a workshop ends? The lessons below come from supporting national and subnational institutions to answer these questions. They do not suggest that every gap has been resolved. They show how risk information can be moved closer to operational decisions, and where sustained leadership is still required. events.summary: Country: Benin Source: Famine Early Warning System Network Please refer to the attached file. Key Messages Stressed (IPC Phase 2) outcomes, with households in Crisis (IPC Phase 3), are expected to persist in northern Benin through May 2027 . Although security incidents have decreased since the beginning of the rainy season, armed groups' activities continue to fuel a climate of fear among civilian populations and are expected to increase during the dry season. Consequently, access to markets and income-generating opportunities is expected to remain limited. Ongoing cereal harvests, as well as those of cash crops at the end of 2026, will progressively improve food availability and agricultural income. However, starting in February 2027, seasonal depletion of stocks, combined with localized deficits, will decrease the availability of staple foods. A proportion of poor or displaced households are expected to increasingly resort to debt, sell productive assets, or be forced to reduce meal portions or frequency. In central and southern Benin, Minimal (IPC Phase 1) outcomes, with very poor households in Stressed (IPC Phase 2), are expected through May 2027. New cereal harvests expected in the main production areas of the north, the primary source of supply for the rest of the country, will strengthen food availability and help maintain a generally sufficient supply in central and southern markets. However, the increase in fuel and transportation costs is expected to progressively increase food and service prices to relatively high levels, reducing the purchasing power of poor households.
